title: Unfinished Mosaic or Honeycomb Quilt Top
medium: Cotton, pieced plain weaves; some printed; some glazed; backed with paper

image.credit: Art Institute of Chicago, Gift of Robert G. Robinson
image.license: Public domain. Released under Creative Commons Zero (CC0) through the Art Institute of Chicago's Open Access program

altText: A square quilt top made of many small hexagon-shaped pieces of printed cotton fabric stitched together like a honeycomb, in a patchwork of warm browns, tans, and other colors and patterns.

context: A quilt top made in the United States around 1840 from pieces of printed and plain cotton, with paper still used as backing. The Art Institute calls it unfinished, meaning it has not yet been layered and stitched into a full quilt. It belongs to the tradition of mosaic or honeycomb patchwork.

descriptions.k: This is a quilt top made of lots of tiny pieces of cloth. Each piece has a small pattern. Can you find a piece with dots or flowers? Imagine sewing all of them together!
descriptions.g12: Long ago someone sewed hundreds of tiny cloth pieces into one big pattern. Each piece has its own print of dots, flowers, or lines. Together they look like a honeycomb. Find a piece you like and tell us about it.
descriptions.g35: This quilt top was made in the United States around 1840 from many small pieces of printed cotton. The pieces are joined into a pattern called mosaic or honeycomb, like a bee's nest. It is called unfinished because it was never turned into a full quilt. How can many small pieces become one big picture?
descriptions.g68: Made in the United States around 1840, this quilt top assembles small pieces of printed and glazed cotton into a mosaic or honeycomb pattern. Paper backing still sits behind the cloth, showing how the pieces were prepared before sewing. Because it is unfinished, we can see the process of making. What does it reveal when a work is shown before it is complete?
descriptions.g910: This c. 1840 American quilt top joins small pieces of printed and glazed cotton in a repeating mosaic or honeycomb arrangement, still backed with paper. As an unfinished object, it preserves the evidence of preparation that a completed quilt would hide. The maker's identity is unknown. How does this piece challenge the idea that art needs a famous name?
descriptions.g1112: This unfinished quilt top (c. 1840), pieced from printed and glazed cotton in a mosaic or honeycomb repetition and still papered on the reverse, makes visible the procedures usually concealed in a finished bedcover. Its maker is anonymous, and its aesthetic rests on accumulation and repetition. How does it complicate hierarchies between fine art and domestic craft, and what does repetition of a single unit achieve?

k.daily: Find two pieces that look different from each other. How are they different?
k.emotion: Does this quilt feel cozy or busy? What makes you feel that way?
k.observation: Count how many pieces you can see in one small area.
k.analysis: Why do you think the pieces fit together so neatly?
k.line: Trace the edge of one piece with your finger. How many sides does it have?
k.shape: What shape is each little piece? Where else have you seen that shape?
k.color: Which colors do you see the most? Point to your favorite.
k.texture: Does this cloth look soft or stiff? Tell us how you know.
k.space: If you folded this quilt top, how big would it be? Show with your arms.
k.light: Do some pieces look lighter and some darker? Where are they?
k.meaning: Why might someone spend so long sewing tiny pieces?
k.culture: People make blankets all around the world. What blanket do you have at home?
k.technique: The maker used needle and thread. How might sewing be like building?
k.personal: If you made a quilt, what picture or color would you put on it?
k.critical: What would you change about the pattern if you were the maker?

g12.daily: Find two pieces of cloth that look different. What is different about them?
g12.emotion: Does this quilt top feel warm and cozy, or busy and loud? Show us where you see that.
g12.observation: Choose one tiny piece and describe its pattern in your own words.
g12.analysis: Why do you think the maker fit so many small pieces together?
g12.line: Follow the edges of the pieces with your finger. What kind of lines do they make?
g12.shape: What shape is repeated all over the quilt top? How many sides does it have?
g12.color: Which colors show up again and again in the quilt top?
g12.texture: Which pieces look smooth and shiny, and which look flat and soft?
g12.space: How would this quilt top look on a bed? Show us its size with your hands.
g12.light: Do you see lighter and darker pieces next to each other? Where?
g12.meaning: Why do you think someone saved scraps of cloth to make this?
g12.culture: Who in your family makes things by hand? What do they make?
g12.technique: The maker used needle and thread to join the pieces. What was the hardest part, do you think?
g12.personal: If you could choose a piece of cloth from your own life to sew in, what would it be?
g12.critical: What would you want to do with this quilt top once it is finished?

g35.daily: Which pieces of cloth do you like best, and what makes them special?
g35.emotion: What mood does this patchwork give you? Point to what makes you feel that way.
g35.observation: Describe three different pieces of fabric you can see. What patterns do they have?
g35.analysis: Why does the pattern look like a honeycomb from far away but like tiny pictures up close?
g35.line: Look at where pieces meet. What lines do you see running across the quilt top?
g35.shape: The pieces have six sides. How does that shape help them fit with no gaps?
g35.color: Which colors repeat across the quilt, and which ones appear only once?
g35.texture: How can you tell this is cloth and not paper or paint?
g35.space: How does the quilt top feel flat but still seem to have a pattern that goes on and on?
g35.light: Where do you see lighter pieces and darker pieces, and how do they make the pattern?
g35.meaning: Why might a person make something this detailed for a bed?
g35.culture: This quilt was made in the United States about 180 years ago. What might it tell us about how people lived?
g35.technique: The pieces were stitched over paper to keep their shape. Why would that help the maker?
g35.personal: If you saved scraps of your old clothes, what would you make from them?
g35.critical: Is a quilt a work of art, a useful object, or both? Give a reason.

g68.daily: Which part of this quilt top would you stop at first, and what draws your eye there?
g68.emotion: What mood do the muted, warm tones create compared with a quilt in bright primary colors?
g68.observation: Choose a small group of pieces and describe how their prints differ from the pieces beside them.
g68.analysis: How does the honeycomb pattern keep your eye moving across the whole surface?
g68.line: How do the edges where pieces join create a network of lines across the quilt?
g68.shape: Why is a six-sided shape such a good choice for covering a flat surface?
g68.color: How do repeated colors help tie together so many different prints?
g68.texture: What do the printed and glazed cotton pieces suggest about the textures the maker handled?
g68.space: How does the pattern create a feeling of depth or flatness at the same time?
g68.light: How do lighter and darker pieces form larger shapes inside the mosaic?
g68.meaning: What does it say about the maker's patience that so many tiny pieces were joined by hand?
g68.culture: How might quilts like this have been part of home life, family, and community in the early 1800s?
g68.technique: The paper pieces are still in place. What does that tell you about how the maker worked?
g68.personal: If you were to finish this quilt top, what steps would still be needed?
g68.critical: How is making a quilt from scraps similar to making a collage, and how is it different?

g910.daily: How does repeating one small unit across the surface produce both unity and variety?
g910.emotion: Why might the muted warm palette give this piece a quiet, domestic mood rather than a dramatic one?
g910.observation: What do the joins between hexagons tell you about the order in which the maker may have worked?
g910.analysis: Analyze how the individual printed fabrics interact to form a larger pattern that is neither random nor rigid.
g910.line: How do the seams function as a visible grid that organizes the composition?
g910.shape: What are the advantages of the hexagon as a module, both practically and visually?
g910.color: How does limited repetition of color help hold together a wide range of prints?
g910.texture: What can the contrast between printed and glazed cottons suggest about the available materials in the 1840s?
g910.space: How does the pattern flatten space while still generating an optical shimmer across the field?
g910.light: How does variation between light and dark pieces create secondary shapes within the honeycomb?
g910.meaning: What does it mean that the maker of this piece is unknown, and how does that affect how we value it?
g910.culture: How might the economic and domestic world of the 1840s shape a patchwork tradition built on small scraps?
g910.technique: How does the paper still attached to the pieces turn the object into evidence of process?
g910.personal: What is gained by showing an unfinished object in a museum rather than a completed quilt?
g910.critical: How would you argue for the place of quilts alongside paintings in the history of design?

g1112.daily: How does the strict modular repetition of the hexagon generate a rhythm that is simultaneously systematic and individualized by each fabric's print?
g1112.emotion: In what ways might a restrained, warm palette produce a mood of domestic quiet while still sustaining visual interest?
g1112.observation: What interpretive possibilities arise from seeing the visible papers and seams as a record of labor rather than as flaws?
g1112.analysis: Evaluate how pattern, color, and scale interact to prevent the field from collapsing into monotony.
g1112.line: How does the network of seams operate as a structural drawing that underlies the textile image?
g1112.shape: Why is the honeycomb module especially suited to the dual demands of efficient piecing and optical complexity?
g1112.color: How does the distribution of color across the surface create a kind of invisible composition above the individual units?
g1112.texture: What does the mixture of printed and glazed cottons suggest about material culture, trade, and household economy around 1840?
g1112.space: How does the all-over pattern resist a single focal point, and what implications does that have for the viewer's movement?
g1112.light: How do value contrasts between pieces produce emergent forms that the maker may or may not have planned?
g1112.meaning: How do anonymity and domestic context challenge conventional assumptions about authorship and artistic status?
g1112.culture: What does the survival of papers in the unfinished top reveal about technique, and why might that matter to historians of textiles?
g1112.technique: Why might museums value process and incompleteness as much as polished final objects?
g1112.personal: What does the scale of labor in this quilt top make you reconsider about the objects you use and overlook every day?
g1112.critical: To what extent should the categories of art, craft, and design determine which objects deserve sustained attention? Use this quilt top as evidence.

teacherNote.context: A quilt top made in the United States around 1840 from pieces of printed and plain cotton, with paper still used as backing. The Art Institute calls it unfinished, meaning it has not yet been layered and stitched into a full quilt. It belongs to the tradition of mosaic or honeycomb patchwork.
directions: Give students paper hexagons or other shapes and have them arrange a patchwork design from colored scraps.
Ask students to describe how a repeated shape can form a larger pattern and to find that effect in the quilt top.
Discuss why a museum might show an unfinished object and what it teaches about how things are made.
